newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Germany says Italy ERM entry not golden key to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Germany says Italy ERM entry not golden key to EMU.

text.p: Germany on Monday welcomed the lira back into the fold of Europe's exchange rate grid, but made clear this vote of confidence did not mean Italy could relax its efforts to impose strict financial discipline.

In a briefing held after two days of gruelling negotiations on terms for the lira's re-entry, top German finance officials said it should not be seen as a sign Italy would automatically join Europe's single currency in 1999.
"This is not a prejudicial decision. It is certainly not a comment on Italy's qualification for monetary union," Tietmeyer told reporters after the talks.
"The challenge now for Italy is to maintain its policy in a way which can allow it to keep its currency steady," he added.
After about 17 hours of weekend talks, the EU ministers agreed to admit the lira at a central rate of 990 lire to the mark, a stronger rate than Italy had hoped for.
Sources said Germany, which believes that a strong currency is proof of a sound economy, was the key opponent of a weaker lira parity during the talks.
The Italians initially asked for a rate of between 1,010 and 1,000 lire to the mark, but finally gave in to a strong EU majority demanding a stronger rate.
In common with most other European countries, Italy is currently scrambling to put its economy into shape in time to qualify for the planned start of European Economic and Monetary Union in 1999.

To join, countries must meet stringent goals on interest and exchange rates, inflation, public deficits and public debt next year. Most, including Italy, are facing the greatest problems in meeting the fiscal criteria.

For Italy, whose currency was kicked out of the ERM by huge waves of speculative selling four years ago, the return to the mechanism offers it a chance to prove it can hold its currency steady for two years before EMU starts.
In a statement released in Bonn welcoming the lira back, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said its return to the ERM boosted the credibility of Italian efforts to streamline the economy.
He also said the parity rate chosen for the lira matched past currency market developments.
But Tietmeyer and Juergen Stark, state secretary to the finance ministry, said Italy's attitude had been a major factor in delaying the agreement.
Italy had come to the talks riding a wave of public statements about its planned re-entry and determined to help its exports by entering at the weaker rate.
Starck said this prevented the EU's monetary commitee on Saturday from reaching a deal, forcing the top level of monetary officials to sort it out the following day.
"We reached no agreement yesterday as Italy had one position and the majority had opposing positions," he said. "There were clear battlelines."
